name: The Second Oak of Summit Woods

location.address: Summit Woods (Bois Summit / Parc Summit), along the main trail near the summit of Westmount hill, City of Westmount

access: Free; Summit Woods is a public park owned by the City of Westmount since 1940 (deeded 'as a park or playground in perpetuity'), open daily with public trails
transport: No metro sits at the summit itself; Vendome or Villa-Maria metro station, then roughly a 25-30 minute uphill walk, or a local Westmount bus toward Summit Circle
story:
When McGill University bought the top of Westmount hill in 1895 to keep it from being built on, this oak was already about thirty years old.

The observatory the university had in mind never went up. In 1940 it sold the hill to the City of Westmount on the condition that the land stay a park or playground in perpetuity, and that deed is why the summit carries hardwood forest instead of houses.

The city's heritage survey measured the tree in 2011 at 114 centimetres through the trunk, roughly 3.6 metres round, and put it at over 145 years then, so over 160 now. It ranked as the second-largest oak in Summit Woods. The wood around it is a red oak, sugar maple and white ash mix that the city calls rare in the Montreal area today, surviving almost nowhere but this mountain.

It stands along the main trail near the summit and can be seen from the path without leaving it. Two more thick red oaks are recorded here, further down a steep unmaintained slope, which is a different kind of walk altogether. A late black cherry grows on the same easy stretch.

The tree's own figures come from that single official survey, which is why the age here is a band rather than a date, and why the pin marks the stretch of trail rather than the exact trunk.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, about 3.6 metres round, the second-thickest oak in the park. It stands beside the main trail near the summit, with a black cherry close by; the other wide oaks are off the path down a steep slope.

name: The Class of '49 Tulip Tree

location.address: McGill University lower campus, in the oval tree planting beside the Redpath Museum, downtown Montreal

access: Free, on open McGill University lower-campus grounds beside the Redpath Museum, publicly walkable, a short walk from the Roddick Gates on Sherbrooke Street
transport: McGill metro station, roughly 5-10 minute walk
story:
McGill's graduating class of 1949 left a tree behind, and it is still standing beside the Redpath Museum.

That makes it unusual company on this map. Almost every tree here carries an estimated age, worked back from a trunk measurement or a register's planting band. This one has a documented year, so the count is simply 77.

A tulip tree is an odd thing to find growing this far north. The species is rare in Quebec and close to the limit of the cold it will take, which is most of the reason the city put this specimen on its remarkable-tree list at all. The survey measured it at 64 centimetres through the trunk, about two metres round. Elsewhere the species reaches three times that thickness, so this is not a giant of its kind; it is a good one in a place where good ones are scarce.

It grows in an oval of mixed species planted around a sunken island of grass on the lower campus, which means it has spent its whole life watching students cut the corner across the same lawn. The black walnut at the Roddick Gates and the ginkgo further into the campus are both a few minutes away, so the three of them make one short errand.

One source documents this tree, the city's own heritage register, and the pin is approximate.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the leaves, cut off flat across the tip as though snipped with scissors, unlike anything else in the row. It stands in the oval of trees around the sunken lawn beside the Redpath Museum.

name: The Roddick Gates Black Walnut

location.address: McGill University lower campus, fronting Sherbrooke Street West near the Roddick Gates, downtown Montreal

access: Free, on open McGill University lower-campus grounds fronting Sherbrooke Street West, immediately inside the publicly accessible Roddick Gates entrance
transport: McGill metro station, roughly 5 minute walk to the Roddick Gates
story:
McGill's own alumni magazine once described this tree as peering in the windows of the Redpath Museum. That was in 2001, and it is still doing it.

The black walnut stands just inside the Roddick Gates, in the line of trees along Sherbrooke Street West at the front of the lower campus. The city's heritage survey puts its trunk at 82 centimetres across at chest height, about 2.6 metres round, and rates both its physiological and its structural health as excellent, which is a generous report card for a tree that has spent its life on the edge of a downtown street.

The age needs a caveat. The survey says it was planted at the turn of the century, a phrase that in French can point at either end of the nineteenth. Read against the same page's own note that the tree is more than a hundred years old, it lands at roughly 1900 to 1910, so over 110 years now. Nobody has narrowed it further, and the band here stays wide because of it.

That is more than a century of students coming through the gates underneath it. Black walnut is not a common street tree in Montreal, and while the species can grow half as thick again as this one, a trunk this size on Sherbrooke Street is worth the two minutes it takes to stop.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the long leaves, a dozen or more narrow leaflets to a stalk, and the dark furrowed trunk about 2.6 metres round. It stands just inside the Roddick Gates, on the Sherbrooke Street side of the lower campus.

name: The Purple Beech of Redpath Hall

location.address: McGill University lower campus, in the tree alignment on the terrace facing Redpath Hall, between the Redpath Library and McLennan Library pavilions, downtown Montreal

access: Free, on open McGill University lower-campus grounds; the Redpath Hall terrace is a publicly walkable outdoor space between the library buildings
transport: McGill metro station, roughly 5-10 minute walk
story:
At roughly 75 years old this is one of the youngest trees on this map, and the city still counts it among the largest purple beeches on Mont-Royal.

That says as much about purple beeches here as it does about this one. It went in around the middle of the twentieth century, part of a mixed row planted along the terrace between the Redpath and McLennan library pavilions, and by the city's own description it matches its neighbours in size and shape. The one thing that separates it from the line is colour: dark purple foliage in a row of ordinary green.

It sits on the axis facing Redpath Hall, finished in 1893 and one of the oldest buildings on the campus, which makes the building comfortably older than the tree looking at it. Generations of students have crossed that terrace between lectures without registering that the odd-coloured one in the row is on a heritage list.

The survey measured it at 56 centimetres through the trunk, about 1.8 metres round, and called it around 60 years old when the work was done in 2011, which is where the 75 comes from. No other source names this tree, so both numbers rest on that single page.

The black walnut at the Roddick Gates, the tulip tree by the Redpath Museum and the ginkgo further up are all a few minutes away.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the colour: dark purple leaves in a row of otherwise green trees of the same size and shape. It stands in the terrace alignment directly facing Redpath Hall, between the two library pavilions.
